talks.title: BSidesCLT 2022: Delivering Control Assurance Through Purple Teaming
talks.teaser: Evaluates BSidesCLT 2022: Delivering Control Assurance Through Purple Teaming and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Purple Teaming Defined

Carlos Rodriguez and Ben Fink contrast vulnerability scans, red teaming, blue teaming, and purple teaming. Purple exercises are collaborative, keyboard-on engagements where red activity is exposed to defenders in real time to improve people, process, and technology together.

Why It Beats Siloed Testing

Unlike traditional red-team reports delivered after the fact, purple teaming creates dialogue during ATT&CK-aligned TTP execution. Blue teams learn whether expensive tools actually detect agreed scenarios or merely consume analyst time.

Control Assurance Benefits

The speakers tie purple teaming to control assurance for leadership: validating detections against behavior-based threat intelligence (e.g., ransomware TTPs), tuning SIEM rules, and training staff. Scale can flex from strategic assessments to narrower technical validations.

Planning and Culture

Success requires shared TTP selection during planning, open communication about what each side observes, and treating outcomes as training—not blame—to strengthen defensive posture.

talks.title: BSidesCLT 2022: Privacy for College Students
talks.teaser: Discusses BSidesCLT 2022: Privacy for College Students and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview:
At BSidesCLT 2022, student and researcher Jessie delivers an analysis of the extensive personal data collected by modern higher education institutions and ed-tech ecosystems. The presentation examines the pervasive privacy risks students face throughout their academic lifecycles, from application portals and financial aid forms to campus Wi-Fi tracking and remote learning tools. Jessie evaluates the legal frameworks governing student records, details major regulatory loopholes, and presents practical operational security strategies to help students safeguard their digital footprint.

Key Topics:
- PII and behavioral data collection across admissions, academic portals, and campus networks.
- Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) protections and statutory loopholes.
- Third-party data sharing and directory information disclosure exemptions.
- Practical student opsec: masked payment cards, credit freezes, VPNs, and account isolation.

Technical Details:
Colleges and universities collect vast repositories of highly sensitive student information, encompassing Social Security numbers, banking details via FAFSA, health and vaccination records, academic transcripts, disciplinary histories, and real-time physical locations gathered via campus Wi-Fi associations. In addition to internal administrative systems, academic programs mandate the installation of third-party software, including learning management systems, messaging platforms, and proctoring tools. These third-party applications expand the institutional attack surface and often enforce opaque data handling policies outside direct student control.

The presentation critically evaluates the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA), the primary federal statute governing student educational records in the United States. While FERPA restricts disclosure without consent once a student turns 18 or matriculates into college, the speaker highlights significant regulatory exemptions. Institutions maintain broad discretion in defining "directory information"—which may include names, addresses, enrollment statuses, and emails—which can be publicly shared unless students formally submit opt-out requests. Crucially, regulatory amendments in 2012 expanded exceptions allowing universities to disclose sensitive records, including Social Security numbers and grades, to external government and evaluation agencies without student knowledge or consent.

To counteract these institutional privacy risks, Jessie outlines a multi-layered defensive strategy. Financially, students can mitigate exposure by avoiding linked primary bank accounts, instead utilizing masked debit cards with transaction limits and imposing credit freezes across major reporting bureaus to prevent identity theft following campus breaches. Digitally, students are advised to maintain strict separation between personal and academic computing by using dedicated devices or browser profiles, routing all campus network traffic through trusted VPNs, enforcing unique credentials via password managers, and regularly pruning historical social media footprints.

Key Takeaways:
Higher education institutions serve as major targets for data harvesting and ransomware attacks due to high concentrations of PII and legacy compliance architectures. Students cannot rely solely on statutory protections like FERPA to preserve their privacy and must proactively exercise formal directory information opt-outs. Implementing practical defense-in-depth measures—such as virtual payment masking, mandatory credit freezes, network traffic encryption, and rigorous credential segmentation—is essential for minimizing exposure while navigating university environments.

talks.title: BSidesCLT 2022: Secrets, Lies, and Half Truths in Cyber Defense
talks.teaser: Analyzes BSidesCLT 2022: Secrets, Lies, and Half Truths in Cyber Defense and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Premise

Mark Orlando (Bionic CEO, SANS instructor) challenges comforting myths in cyber defense, arguing rising spend has not matched improvement in security operations outcomes.

Self-deception themes

He satirizes beliefs that smart hires, shiny RSA expo tools, comprehensive metrics, or dismissing alerts as noise guarantee resilience—especially after breaches despite completed risk matrices.

Teamwork reality

Effective teams need deliberate collaboration, shared skill-building, and measured interactions—not just assembling capable individuals who may drift or dominate incidents.

Egocentrism and complexity

Security's ego-driven solo responders and multi-team dependencies undermine coordination; cloud or IR problems require cross-functional effort no single analyst can own.

Goal

Replace half-truths with ground truth and repeatable practices for building, executing, and managing defense programs.

talks.title: BSidesCLT 2022: Breaking the Giants with Logic
talks.teaser: Provides BSidesCLT 2022: Breaking the Giants with Logic and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Logic Bugs on Major Platforms

Ali Khabil presents the second installment of "Breaking the Giants with Logic" at BSides Charlotte, continuing his bug-bounty research into business-logic flaws on large web properties. Unlike code-level RCE or XSS, these vulnerabilities exploit application workflows—pricing, loyalty points, account state—that developers overlook.

## Why Duplicates Dominate Bounty Programs

Duplicate reports frustrate hunters who invest hours only to learn someone filed the same issue first. Khabil argues the bounty economy over-rewards classic injection bugs while under-exploring logic paths, causing crowded competition on identical attack surfaces.

## Bare-Handed Exploitation Techniques

"Bare-handed" means manipulating normal API behavior without exotic payloads: negative purchase amounts, point-multiplication races, or loyalty-program arithmetic that turns $100 spent into thousands of redeemable credits. Real shops define reward ratios; attackers subvert the math.

## Hunting Beyond the Code Layer

Effective logic testing requires understanding business rules, state machines, and race conditions across checkout, refunds, and promotions. Khabil encourages researchers to model how money and entitlements flow through an application rather than scanning only for syntactic vulnerabilities.
